title: The peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:7)
hookLine: being a good citizen wherever you live
tomorrow: what's the first question a life gets asked at the end?

cards: A notice taped to the library door: park cleanup Saturday, volunteers wanted. It's easy to walk past, especially in a town you'll be leaving soon.
The prophet Jeremiah once wrote to people who wanted to leave far more than that. Exiles, carried off to Babylon, the capital of the empire that had taken them. They expected to go home any day.
His letter tells them something they didn't want to hear: unpack.

teach.b: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them."

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THAT CITY.
teach.b: Then the line that stops you: "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Not their own city.
Babylon. The place they never chose. Seek its peace, and pray for it, because their peace is tied up with their neighbors' peace.
The Mishnah carries the idea forward.
Rabbi Chanina, the deputy of the priests, says: pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow each other alive. That's not praise for any ruler.
It's a plain point that order protects people who can't protect themselves. So what does a good citizen look like here?
Someone who plants where they are. Who shows up for the cleanup, the food drive, the library shelf, the town meeting, even in a place that may not be home forever.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Bible's line about seeking a city's peace was written to captives, about the very city that held them.

how: Jewish tradition draws on Jeremiah 29:7 for seeking the welfare of the place where Jews live, and some synagogues include a prayer for the country and its government in their Shabbat service.

games.q: what does “the peace of the city” mean?
o: keeping quiet so your town stays calm
praying for Jerusalem from wherever you are
caring for the good of the place where you live

games.q: a letter to the exiles — tap the pairs.

s: Jeremiah told the exiles not to unpack, since they'd be home soon
build houses, plant gardens, and seek the peace of the city.
the city in Jeremiah's letter is the exiles' own Jerusalem
it's the city they were carried away to.
a sage of the Mishnah says to pray for the welfare of the government
Rabbi Chanina: without it, people would swallow each other alive.

games.q: you've moved to a new city for a job you'll keep about a year. a neighbor asks you to help at the block's food drive. what fits Jeremiah's letter?
o: help: seek the peace of the place you live, even for a while.
leave it to people who plan to stay; it's really their city.
pray for the city, but keep out of its everyday life.
games.why: Jeremiah wrote to people who expected to leave: build, plant, and seek the city's peace, for in its peace you'll have peace.

practice: Walk to a window or your front door, and spend a minute just looking at your street. Notice one thing that could be better: a sidewalk, a neighbor who's often alone, a sign asking for help.
Name one small thing you could do for this place, whether you'll live here a long time or not.

wordCard.voice: The peace of the city: Jeremiah's charge to the exiles, to seek the good of the place where you live, because your peace is tied to its peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: the peace of the city, from Jeremiah 29:7.

carryVoice: Your line: seek the city's peace. Plant a garden where you are, even for a season. Talk soon.
